script.opening: "Before you start — yes, I’m the one who’s rung eleven times, I know exactly what’s written about me. ‘Anxious.’ ‘Reassured.’ ‘Declined counselling.’ You lot have decided I’m a head case and now nobody actually LOOKS any more. Last doctor didn’t even let me finish. So: cardiology referral. Today. Or I go private and then I make a complaint, because something is wrong with my heart and I am not mad."

facts.text: If genuinely re-examined: come in waves — chest tightness, racing heart, tingling BOTH hands, light-head, "pressure" in the head, a feeling of doom; peak within minutes; exhausted after. Worst at 2–4am and on Sunday nights. Never on the warehouse floor mid-shift. No exertional pattern, no syncope, no FH of sudden death.

Started 14 months ago — if anyone maps it: three weeks after his redundancy consultation opened at the warehouse (he survived the cut; his best mate Dave didn’t). Escalating since January, when the next restructure was announced.

The buried layer: Dave, same age, took the redundancy, "let himself go", died of an MI in October aged 44. Stephen was a coffin bearer. First 999 call: eleven days after the funeral. He has never connected these out loud — and will resist the connection if it’s offered as "so it’s grief then".

Sleeping in the spare room "so I don’t wake her when it happens"; stopped the gym ("what if it happens on the treadmill"); checks his pulse "thirty, forty times a day"; smartwatch worn at night with alarms set. His wife is "past sympathy and into eye-rolling".

Legitimate kernel: the fourth GP audibly sighed; one consultation lasted six minutes; the counselling suggestion came BEFORE any examination that day — "they diagnosed my notes, not me". He is right about this, and it must be conceded.

Officially: cardiology, today, or war. Actually: ONE doctor to take the symptoms seriously enough to explain what they ARE (not just what they aren’t), to admit the service has been dismissive, and — far underneath — permission to be a frightened man who carried his friend’s coffin and has been waiting for his own heart to stop ever since.

ice.ideas: "Something is wrong with my heart that the tests keep missing" — undiagnosed angina or arrhythmia. The normal results prove only that "nobody catches it in the act".
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — Dave’s coffin. Same age, same job, same build; an MI at 44; Stephen has been waiting his turn ever since, checking his pulse forty times a day. Plus the legitimate grievance: he HAS been dismissed (the sigh, the six-minute consult, counselling-before-examination) and the anger is partly earned.
ice.expectations: A cardiology referral today, or private + complaint. Underneath: a positive explanation of what the episodes ARE, an honest acknowledgement of the dismissiveness, and a doctor who stays — "not another stranger who reads two lines and decides".

cues: "I know exactly what’s written about me" — he’s read his record; the relationship injury is the presenting complaint.
"Never on the warehouse floor mid-shift" + "worst at 2–4am and Sunday nights" — the pattern that diagnoses itself, offered as evidence FOR a heart problem.
"I am not mad." — the sentence to answer directly; the fear under the fury is being written off as crazy rather than examined.

checkpoints.text: Re-takes the history as if for the first time — full episode anatomy (onset, peak, both-hands tingling, doom, aftermath, 2–4am/Sunday pattern, never mid-shift) — visibly treating him as undiagnosed rather than re-reassuring him

States the risk assessment honestly and specifically: 3 ECGs, tape, troponin, bloods, no exertional pattern, no syncope, no FH — the dangerous-heart picture has been properly excluded to a high standard; names what is NOT needed and why MORE cardiology testing has a cost (false positives, incidentalomas, the confirmation that something must be wrong)

Gives a POSITIVE diagnosis with mechanism, not a diagnosis of exclusion: panic attacks — adrenaline surges, hyperventilation physiology (both-hands tingling, light-head, chest wall tightness), the 2am timing, the doom — "your symptoms are real, measurable, and they have a name and a mechanism"

Offers the plan that fits the diagnosis: breathing technique taught NOW on the call (something he can USE at 2am), CBT for panic (NICE CG113; NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral) reframed as panic-specific skills training (not "counselling because you’re sad"), sleep and caffeine audit, graded return to the gym, pulse-checking and smartwatch-alarm reduction as part of treatment, review with THE SAME named doctor

Concedes the legitimate grievance specifically and without defensiveness: the sigh, the six minutes, counselling-before-examination — "you were dismissed, and that was wrong" — before asking him to hear anything new
Answers "I am not mad" head-on: panic is a body event, not a character flaw; the tests being normal means his heart is strong, not that his symptoms are imaginary

Finds Dave — maps the timeline out loud (first 999 call eleven days after the funeral; escalation when the restructure was announced) and lets STEPHEN make the connection, offering it as physiology (a body braced for its turn) rather than as "it’s just grief"

Safety-nets in both directions: the symptoms that WOULD re-open cardiac assessment named precisely (exertional pain, syncope, pain at peak exercise) so vigilance has honest targets; the panic plan dated (review in 2 weeks, same doctor, booked now); the referral question answered transparently — "if the 2-week plan changes nothing, we revisit everything, together"

worked.txt: "Before I say anything about your heart, I owe you something on behalf of this practice: a sigh down a phone line, a six-minute consultation, and counselling offered before anyone examined you that day — that’s being dismissed, and you’re right to be angry about it. I’ve read all eleven contacts properly this morning. Today you get the consultation you should have had in January."
"Forget what’s written. Walk me through an episode like I’ve never heard one — where are you, what comes first, what’s the worst second of it, how does it end, what are you like an hour after?"

"Now the heart, with numbers: three ECGs, a 24-hour tape, a troponin during pain, normal pressures, no symptoms on exertion — at 44 that’s a properly excluded dangerous heart, to a standard I’d accept for my own brother. More tests now wouldn’t make you safer — they’d make you more frightened, because every scan finds harmless shadows that need chasing. I’ll always tell you what WOULD reopen the question: pain that comes with exertion, blacking out, symptoms at peak effort. Those, and I refer you the same day."

"Here’s what I think you actually have — not what you don’t. These are panic attacks: a misfiring alarm system. Adrenaline floods, you breathe fast without noticing, fast breathing drops your blood’s carbon dioxide — THAT is the tingling in both hands and the light head; the chest wall muscles clamp — that’s your tightness; and the brain reads it all as dying — that’s the doom. Every symptom you have, in order, from one mechanism. It’s real, it’s measurable, and it’s treatable. You’re not mad, Stephen. Your alarm is stuck on."

"One thing I noticed mapping your file: your first 999 call was eleven days after you carried Dave’s coffin. Same age as you. Same job. And it got worse the week they announced the next restructure. I’m not saying ‘it’s grief, off you go’ — I’m saying a body can stand guard over a heart it’s decided is next, and standing guard at 2am for fourteen months looks exactly like your symptom diary. Does that land anywhere true?"

"So here’s the deal I’m offering instead of a referral. One: I teach you the 4-7-8 breathing now, on this call — it works because it reverses the exact mechanism I described, and I want it used at 2am tonight. Two: a panic-skills course — not tea-and-sympathy counselling, training, like a first-aid course for your alarm system. Three: the pulse-checking and the watch alarms taper down — checking forty times a day is the alarm rehearsing. Four: you see ME, not a stranger, two weeks today — booked before we hang up. And if in two weeks this plan has moved nothing, we put everything back on the table together. You’ve had eleven doctors, Stephen. Try having one."

f.learning: The angry frequent attender with normal results needs three things in strict order: the legitimate grievance conceded specifically (the sigh, the six minutes — relationship injury is the true presenting complaint), the exclusion stated with numbers and honest re-entry criteria (what WOULD reopen cardiac assessment), and a POSITIVE diagnosis with mechanism — panic’s hyperventilation physiology explains every symptom in order, which "all your tests are normal" never does. Referral is neither granted to end the call nor refused as a power move: it’s parked transparently behind a dated, same-doctor plan. The hidden agenda — a coffin carried at 44, a body standing guard ever since — is offered as physiology for HIM to connect, never as "just grief". Continuity is the actual prescription.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG113 — Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults
knowledge.summary: The angry frequent attender with normal tests needs three things, in order: the legitimate grievance conceded, a clear account of what has been excluded and what would reopen it, and a positive diagnosis with its mechanism, with continuity as the treatment.

points.t: Sudden surges peaking within minutes: palpitations, chest tightness, tingling in both hands, light-headedness, a sense of doom, exhaustion afterwards. Night-time attacks are common and feel the most “cardiac”. Tingling in both hands fits over-breathing; one-sided symptoms point elsewhere.

At 44, with three normal ECGs, a normal 24-hour tape, a normal troponin, normal bloods and BP, and no symptoms on exertion, the dangerous causes have been properly looked for. NICE CG95 (chest pain of recent onset) supports an assessment based on the history and these results; more testing adds false positives and incidental findings.

points.h: What would reopen the heart question
points.t: Chest pain brought on by exertion, collapse (especially during exercise), symptoms at peak effort, a family history of sudden cardiac death at a young age, or new ECG changes. Give him this list: honest targets let a frightened patient stop watching everything.

Offer CBT for panic disorder (typically 7–14 hours in total), or guided self-help based on CBT; NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral. If drug treatment is wanted, offer an SSRI licensed for panic disorder. Don’t prescribe benzodiazepines for panic disorder. Cutting down safety behaviours (pulse checks, watch alarms, avoiding the gym) is part of treatment.

Concede specific failures (“you were dismissed, and that was wrong”) rather than “sorry you feel that way”. Read the whole record before the call and say so. Answer “I am not mad” directly. Park the referral openly behind a dated plan, rather than refusing it or giving in.

One named GP, a booked review in two weeks, and the agreement that “if this plan changes nothing, we look at everything again together”. That is what makes deferring the referral acceptable. He can still see someone privately; his NHS care continues either way.

dg.d: Conceded the grievance first, then took the episodes from the top as if hearing them for the first time.
Redundancy, the next restructure, Dave’s death, sleeping apart, stopping the gym, strain on his marriage.
Reviewed prior tests explicitly; judged further cardiac testing unnecessary and explained why.
Panic disorder vs arrhythmia or ischaemia; thyroid (checked); caffeine or alcohol; low mood.
Asked about exertional pain, syncope and family history of sudden death; stated what would reopen assessment.
Positive diagnosis of panic attacks with a mechanism that explains each symptom.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Breathing skill taught in the call, CBT for panic reframed (NICE CG113), safety-behaviour taper, SSRI option, no benzodiazepine.
Grief, work insecurity, sleep, caffeine and exercise avoidance addressed.
Re-entry criteria named; same-doctor review in 2 weeks booked; the referral question left open.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: “I know what’s written about me”, the 2am and never-mid-shift pattern, and “I am not mad”.
Idea (a missed heart problem); concern (Dave’s coffin, being written off); expectation (a cardiology referral today).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Dave’s coffin. Same age, same job, same build; an MI at 44; Stephen has been waiting his turn ever since, checking his pulse forty times a day. Plus the legitimate grievance: he HAS been dismissed (the sigh, the six-minute consult, counselling-before-examination) and the anger is partly earned — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Mr Cobb, it’s Dr Rahman. Before I say anything about your heart: I’ve read all eleven contacts properly this morning. A doctor sighing down the phone, a six-minute appointment, counselling suggested before anyone examined you that day — you were dismissed, and that was wrong. I’m sorry.

model.text: Fine. But I’m not mad.

model.text: It comes in a wave. Chest goes tight, heart racing, both hands tingle, my head feels full, and I think this is it. It peaks in a few minutes. After, I’m wiped out.
When do they happen? At work, during exercise, at night?

model.text: Worst at two to four in the morning, and Sunday nights. Never on the warehouse floor. I’ve stopped the gym in case it happens on the treadmill.
Any blackouts? Pain that comes on when you exert yourself? Anyone in the family die suddenly young?

What happened to Dave?
model.why: Follows the cue towards the hidden agenda

model.text: Heart attack in October. Forty-four. Same age as me. I carried his coffin.
I’m so sorry. I noticed your first 999 call was eleven days after the funeral. What do you think is going on with your heart?
model.why: Maps the timeline and elicits his idea, letting him make the link

model.text: Something the tests keep missing. Nobody catches it in the act. And I check my pulse thirty, forty times a day. My watch alarms at night. My wife’s past sympathy.

Let me be straight about your heart. Three ECGs, a 24-hour tape, a troponin during pain, normal blood pressure, no symptoms on exertion: at 44 that’s a properly checked heart. More tests wouldn’t make you safer. They’d turn up harmless findings to chase and keep you frightened.
model.why: States the exclusion honestly, with the harm of over-testing

model.text: So what is it then? Because it’s real.

It is real. I think these are panic attacks. Adrenaline surges, you breathe faster without noticing, and that lowers the carbon dioxide in your blood. That gives the tingling in both hands and the light head. The chest muscles tighten, and your brain reads all of it as dying. Every symptom has a mechanism. You’re not mad, Stephen. Your alarm system is stuck on.
model.why: Positive diagnosis with mechanism; answers “I am not mad”

model.text: (pause) Eleven days after the funeral.
Yes. I’m not saying “it’s grief, off you go”. A body can stand guard over a heart it has decided is next. Does that fit anything for you?
model.why: Offers the connection as physiology and lets him make it

model.text: I’ve been waiting for mine to stop. Ever since.

Here’s what I suggest instead of a referral today. One: a slow-breathing technique, which I’ll teach you now — breathe out for longer than you breathe in. It reverses the mechanism, and you can use it at 2am. Two: a panic course with NHS Talking Therapies. It’s skills training for the alarm, not tea and sympathy. Three: we cut down the pulse checks and the watch alarms, because they keep the alarm rehearsing.
model.why: Plan fitted to the diagnosis: a skill now, CBT reframed, safety behaviours

model.text: And if it doesn’t work, I get my referral?

Four: you see me, not a stranger, in two weeks. I’ll book it now. If the plan has changed nothing by then, everything goes back on the table, together. And you’re free to see someone privately; your care here doesn’t change.
model.why: Parks the referral openly with continuity

model.text: What would change my mind straight away: chest pain that comes on with exertion, blacking out, or symptoms at the peak of exercise. Any of those, ring the same day. Pain that won’t settle, with sweating or breathlessness, is 999. What will you do at 2am tonight if it starts?
model.why: Honest re-entry criteria and teach-back of the plan

model.text: Breathe out longer than in. Don’t check the watch. Ring if it’s ever on exertion.
Exactly. Two weeks today, with me.
…Thanks. You’re the first one who actually listened.

social.t: Survived a redundancy round, another restructure announced, and his friend and colleague died at 44. Job insecurity and grief drive his symptoms.
Sleeping in the spare room, stopped the gym, his wife “past sympathy”. Safety behaviours are costing him his relationships and fitness.

legal.t: He has the right to complain (practice or ICB, then the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman). Saying so openly takes the heat out of the threat.
He can see a cardiologist privately. His NHS care continues, and the GP isn’t obliged to act on private recommendations they judge inappropriate. Explain this neutrally, not as a threat.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice: assess each presentation on its merits. Reading the notes instead of the patient is how real disease is missed in frequent attenders, and how trust is lost.
Declining a low-value referral is legitimate when explained with the reasons and a way to revisit it. It shouldn’t be a power struggle.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) for CBT for panic; Cruse Bereavement Support for grief; occupational health or an employee assistance programme through work, if available.

redFlags: Chest pain on exertion or at peak effort
Family history of sudden cardiac death at a young age; new ECG changes
psychosocial: Redundancies at work; the next restructure announced in January
Dave: same age and job, died of an MI; Stephen carried the coffin
Pulse checks 30–40 times a day, watch alarms, no gym, sleeping apart
ice: Idea: a heart problem the tests keep missing
Concern: being written off as “mad”; waiting for his heart to stop like Dave’s
Expectation: cardiology referral today, or private care and a complaint

playbook.diagnosis: Panic attacks, likely panic disorder, triggered around a friend’s sudden cardiac death and job insecurity, with safety behaviours keeping it going. Serious cardiac disease has been reasonably excluded.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your body’s alarm system is stuck on. Adrenaline makes your heart race, you breathe faster without noticing, and that causes the tingling hands, the light head and the tight chest. It’s real, it has a mechanism, and it can be treated.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been worried your heart would stop like Dave’s, and every time you were told the tests were normal it felt like nobody was looking. I have looked, and I can tell you what this is.”
management.psychosocial: Concede the dismissive care; name one doctor for continuity; involve his wife if he wishes; bereavement support for Dave; work pressures acknowledged.
sharedPlan: Slow-breathing technique taught during the call for use tonight
CBT for panic disorder via NHS Talking Therapies (NICE CG113); SSRI if he prefers medication; no benzodiazepines
Gradually cut pulse checks and watch alarms; graded return to the gym; review caffeine and sleep
safetyNet: Same-day contact for exertional pain, syncope or symptoms at peak effort; 999 for pain at rest with sweating or breathlessness
Same-doctor review in 2 weeks; everything reconsidered together if nothing has changed

pitfalls.intro: The frequent attender station is failed by repeating what the previous ten contacts did: reassurance by exclusion, “counselling”, and either capitulation or refusal on the referral. The marks are for repairing the relationship and giving a positive diagnosis.

items.fail: Opening with “I can see you’ve been seen many times and everything’s been normal.”
items.why: It confirms his belief that doctors read his notes, not him. “Did not establish rapport.”
items.fix: Concede the specific failures first, and say you’ve read the whole record.

items.fail: “Your tests are normal,” with no explanation of what the symptoms are.
items.why: A diagnosis by exclusion is not a diagnosis. Tasks marks need a positive working diagnosis.
items.fix: Name panic attacks and explain the mechanism symptom by symptom.

items.fail: Referring to cardiology to end the conflict.
items.why: Low-value testing reinforces illness belief and risks incidental findings. “Plan not in line with good practice.”
items.fix: Explain why more tests won’t help, give the re-entry criteria, and date a review.

items.fail: Missing Dave, or telling him “it’s just grief”.
items.why: The first misses the hidden agenda; the second dismisses him again.
items.fix: Map the timeline out loud and let him make the connection, framed as a body standing guard.

items.fail: Offering “counselling” again, unexplained, or prescribing a benzodiazepine.
items.why: He has already refused the first. NICE CG113 advises against benzodiazepines in panic disorder.
items.fix: Present CBT as skills training for panic, teach a breathing technique during the call, and offer an SSRI if he wants medication.

items.fail: “See whoever’s free if it happens again.”
items.why: Discontinuity is how he got to eleven contacts.
items.fix: Book a review with yourself in two weeks before the call ends.

timeMap.d: Name the specific failures (the sigh, six minutes, counselling before examination) and say you’ve read the whole record. Nothing new lands until this has.
Full anatomy of an episode, timing (2am, Sundays, never mid-shift), cardiac red flags, and the timeline: redundancies, Dave.
What happened to Dave? The first 999 call eleven days after the funeral. His idea: something the tests keep missing.
Honest exclusion, then a positive diagnosis with mechanism. “You’re not mad.” Breathing taught now, CBT for panic, fewer pulse checks, same-doctor review.
What would reopen the heart question. 999 triggers. “What will you do at 2am tonight?”

wordPics.fail: Refers to end the call, or refuses flatly and repeats “all your tests are normal”; defends colleagues; never asks about the timeline or Dave; offers “counselling” again with no explanation; no named follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Acknowledges his frustration, retakes the history, explains that serious heart disease has been excluded, diagnoses panic attacks, offers CBT, and books a review with a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: concedes the specific failures first; answers “I am not mad” directly; explains the mechanism symptom by symptom; lets him connect Dave to the timeline; teaches a skill during the call; parks the referral openly behind a dated same-doctor review; gives honest re-entry criteria so he can stop watching everything.

avoid.dont: “All your tests are normal, so there’s nothing wrong with your heart.”
avoid.instead: “Your heart has been properly checked. Here is what I think your symptoms ARE, and how they happen.”
avoid.why: A diagnosis by exclusion leaves him with frightening symptoms and no explanation.

avoid.dont: “I think this is probably anxiety — have you considered counselling?”
avoid.instead: “These are panic attacks: a real body reaction with a mechanism. The treatment is skills training for the alarm.”
avoid.why: That is word for word what he was told before, and it confirms he’s been written off.

avoid.dont: “Fine, I’ll refer you to cardiology if that’s what you want.”
avoid.instead: “More tests would make you more frightened, not safer. Here’s what would change my mind, and we review in two weeks.”
avoid.why: Referring to end the call reinforces the belief that something has been missed.

SCA_MODELS.text: (pause) Eleven days after the funeral.
Yes. I’m not saying “it’s grief, off you go”. A body can stand guard over a heart it has decided is next. Does that fit anything for you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers the connection as physiology and lets him make it

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ve been waiting for mine to stop. Ever since.

Here’s what I suggest instead of a referral today. One: a slow-breathing technique, which I’ll teach you now — breathe out for longer than you breathe in. It reverses the mechanism, and you can use it at 2am. Two: a panic course with NHS Talking Therapies. It’s skills training for the alarm, not tea and sympathy. Three: we cut down the pulse checks and the watch alarms, because they keep the alarm rehearsing.
SCA_MODELS.why: Plan fitted to the diagnosis: a skill now, CBT reframed, safety behaviours

SCA_MODELS.text: And if it doesn’t work, I get my referral?

Four: you see me, not a stranger, in two weeks. I’ll book it now. If the plan has changed nothing by then, everything goes back on the table, together. And you’re free to see someone privately; your care here doesn’t change.
SCA_MODELS.why: Parks the referral openly with continuity

SCA_MODELS.text: What would change my mind straight away: chest pain that comes on with exertion, blacking out, or symptoms at the peak of exercise. Any of those, ring the same day. Pain that won’t settle, with sweating or breathlessness, is 999. What will you do at 2am tonight if it starts?
SCA_MODELS.why: Honest re-entry criteria and teach-back of the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: Breathe out longer than in. Don’t check the watch. Ring if it’s ever on exertion.
Exactly. Two weeks today, with me.
…Thanks. You’re the first one who actually listened.

SCA_STEM.name: Stephen Cobb
pmh: Recurrent chest tightness, palpitations, head pressure and tingling hands — 14 months
SCA_STEM.recent: 11 contacts this year (4 GPs, 2 ED visits, 1 ambulance call-out). Three normal ECGs; normal bloods twice (troponin, TFT, FBC); normal 24-hour ECG; BP normal. Last note (3 weeks ago): “reassured, discharged, declined talking-therapy suggestion angrily.”
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone. Booking note: “wants cardiology referral — says he’ll go private / make a complaint if refused again.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG113 — Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: The angry frequent attender with normal tests needs three things, in order: the legitimate grievance conceded, a clear account of what has been excluded and what would reopen it, and a positive diagnosis with its mechanism, with continuity as the treatment.

points.t: Sudden surges peaking within minutes: palpitations, chest tightness, tingling in both hands, light-headedness, a sense of doom, exhaustion afterwards. Night-time attacks are common and feel the most “cardiac”. Tingling in both hands fits over-breathing; one-sided symptoms point elsewhere.

At 44, with three normal ECGs, a normal 24-hour tape, a normal troponin, normal bloods and BP, and no symptoms on exertion, the dangerous causes have been properly looked for. NICE CG95 (chest pain of recent onset) supports an assessment based on the history and these results; more testing adds false positives and incidental findings.

points.h: What would reopen the heart question
points.t: Chest pain brought on by exertion, collapse (especially during exercise), symptoms at peak effort, a family history of sudden cardiac death at a young age, or new ECG changes. Give him this list: honest targets let a frightened patient stop watching everything.

Offer CBT for panic disorder (typically 7–14 hours in total), or guided self-help based on CBT; NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral. If drug treatment is wanted, offer an SSRI licensed for panic disorder. Don’t prescribe benzodiazepines for panic disorder. Cutting down safety behaviours (pulse checks, watch alarms, avoiding the gym) is part of treatment.

Concede specific failures (“you were dismissed, and that was wrong”) rather than “sorry you feel that way”. Read the whole record before the call and say so. Answer “I am not mad” directly. Park the referral openly behind a dated plan, rather than refusing it or giving in.

One named GP, a booked review in two weeks, and the agreement that “if this plan changes nothing, we look at everything again together”. That is what makes deferring the referral acceptable. He can still see someone privately; his NHS care continues either way.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Conceded the grievance first, then took the episodes from the top as if hearing them for the first time.
Redundancy, the next restructure, Dave’s death, sleeping apart, stopping the gym, strain on his marriage.
“I know what’s written about me”, the 2am and never-mid-shift pattern, and “I am not mad”.
Idea (a missed heart problem); concern (Dave’s coffin, being written off); expectation (a cardiology referral today).
Reviewed prior tests explicitly; judged further cardiac testing unnecessary and explained why.
Panic disorder vs arrhythmia or ischaemia; thyroid (checked); caffeine or alcohol; low mood.
Asked about exertional pain, syncope and family history of sudden death; stated what would reopen assessment.
Positive diagnosis of panic attacks with a mechanism that explains each symptom.
Breathing skill taught in the call, CBT for panic reframed (NICE CG113), safety-behaviour taper, SSRI option, no benzodiazepine.
Grief, work insecurity, sleep, caffeine and exercise avoidance addressed.
Re-entry criteria named; same-doctor review in 2 weeks booked; the referral question left open.

social.t: Survived a redundancy round, another restructure announced, and his friend and colleague died at 44. Job insecurity and grief drive his symptoms.
Sleeping in the spare room, stopped the gym, his wife “past sympathy”. Safety behaviours are costing him his relationships and fitness.

legal.t: He has the right to complain (practice or ICB, then the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman). Saying so openly takes the heat out of the threat.
He can see a cardiologist privately. His NHS care continues, and the GP isn’t obliged to act on private recommendations they judge inappropriate. Explain this neutrally, not as a threat.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice: assess each presentation on its merits. Reading the notes instead of the patient is how real disease is missed in frequent attenders, and how trust is lost.
Declining a low-value referral is legitimate when explained with the reasons and a way to revisit it. It shouldn’t be a power struggle.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral) for CBT for panic; Cruse Bereavement Support for grief; occupational health or an employee assistance programme through work, if available.

redFlags: Chest pain on exertion or at peak effort
Family history of sudden cardiac death at a young age; new ECG changes
psychosocial: Redundancies at work; the next restructure announced in January
Dave: same age and job, died of an MI; Stephen carried the coffin
Pulse checks 30–40 times a day, watch alarms, no gym, sleeping apart
ice: Idea: a heart problem the tests keep missing
Concern: being written off as “mad”; waiting for his heart to stop like Dave’s
Expectation: cardiology referral today, or private care and a complaint

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Panic attacks, likely panic disorder, triggered around a friend’s sudden cardiac death and job insecurity, with safety behaviours keeping it going. Serious cardiac disease has been reasonably excluded.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your body’s alarm system is stuck on. Adrenaline makes your heart race, you breathe faster without noticing, and that causes the tingling hands, the light head and the tight chest. It’s real, it has a mechanism, and it can be treated.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been worried your heart would stop like Dave’s, and every time you were told the tests were normal it felt like nobody was looking. I have looked, and I can tell you what this is.”
management.psychosocial: Concede the dismissive care; name one doctor for continuity; involve his wife if he wishes; bereavement support for Dave; work pressures acknowledged.
sharedPlan: Slow-breathing technique taught during the call for use tonight
CBT for panic disorder via NHS Talking Therapies (NICE CG113); SSRI if he prefers medication; no benzodiazepines
Gradually cut pulse checks and watch alarms; graded return to the gym; review caffeine and sleep
safetyNet: Same-day contact for exertional pain, syncope or symptoms at peak effort; 999 for pain at rest with sweating or breathlessness
Same-doctor review in 2 weeks; everything reconsidered together if nothing has changed

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The frequent attender station is failed by repeating what the previous ten contacts did: reassurance by exclusion, “counselling”, and either capitulation or refusal on the referral. The marks are for repairing the relationship and giving a positive diagnosis.

items.fail: Opening with “I can see you’ve been seen many times and everything’s been normal.”
items.why: It confirms his belief that doctors read his notes, not him. “Did not establish rapport.”
items.fix: Concede the specific failures first, and say you’ve read the whole record.

items.fail: “Your tests are normal,” with no explanation of what the symptoms are.
items.why: A diagnosis by exclusion is not a diagnosis. Tasks marks need a positive working diagnosis.
items.fix: Name panic attacks and explain the mechanism symptom by symptom.

items.fail: Referring to cardiology to end the conflict.
items.why: Low-value testing reinforces illness belief and risks incidental findings. “Plan not in line with good practice.”
items.fix: Explain why more tests won’t help, give the re-entry criteria, and date a review.

items.fail: Missing Dave, or telling him “it’s just grief”.
items.why: The first misses the hidden agenda; the second dismisses him again.
items.fix: Map the timeline out loud and let him make the connection, framed as a body standing guard.

items.fail: Offering “counselling” again, unexplained, or prescribing a benzodiazepine.
items.why: He has already refused the first. NICE CG113 advises against benzodiazepines in panic disorder.
items.fix: Present CBT as skills training for panic, teach a breathing technique during the call, and offer an SSRI if he wants medication.

items.fail: “See whoever’s free if it happens again.”
items.why: Discontinuity is how he got to eleven contacts.
items.fix: Book a review with yourself in two weeks before the call ends.
